implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits the JVM monitor through the standard library's inline synchronized function, so the compiler-bound block release of Java is available unchanged; on top of that, kotlin.concurrent.withLock gives java.util.concurrent locks the same containment - it locks, runs the lambda and unlocks in a finally, so Lock users keep timed or interruptible acquisition without hand-written try/finally. ReentrantReadWriteLock gains read {}/write {} the same way. Explicit lock()/unlock() survives only when the lock must be handed off between scopes, which a lambda cannot express.
pitfalls: synchronized and withLock block the calling thread; calling them from a coroutine blocks the dispatcher thread and can deadlock a single-threaded dispatcher.
withLock is inline, so a non-local return from the lambda still unlocks, but a manual lock() call inside the lambda followed by an exception leaks the lock.
Synchronizing on a public object, on a companion or on an interned String exposes the monitor; use a private lock instance.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex.withLock
variants.implementation_notes: For suspending code the structural lock is kotlinx.coroutines' Mutex: withLock is a suspend function that acquires the mutex, runs the suspending lambda and releases it in a finally, so waiting coroutines suspend instead of blocking threads and the guard may be held across suspension points. This is the variant to use when the guarded work awaits - database, network - while keeping the critical section expressed as a single block. kotlinx Mutex is not reentrant, so a nested withLock on the same mutex suspends forever.
pitfalls: Mutex is not reentrant: a nested withLock on the same mutex suspends the coroutine forever rather than failing.
Holding the mutex across suspension points serializes every coroutine that wants it; it is right for a critical section and wrong for a cache that should run concurrently.
Mixing Mutex (coroutine-aware) with synchronized (thread-blocking) around the same state gives no mutual exclusion between the two worlds.
